name: sun_clock_realistic_moon
_comment: Proves the §14 day-length SETTING carries the moon with it: flipping 'Vanilla day length' to
'Realistic day length' must re-time the sun AND the moon together, not just the sun.
Why this needs a live scenario. MoonPosition takes its day percent out of SolarPosition.Inputs,
so the coupling is a property of two adapters that both take a live Map — SunClockModeMoonTests
can only mirror that composition offline, and would stay green if MoonPosition were rewired back
to GenLocalDate.DayPercent. This file drives the real ones. It is also the first scenario to
exercise realistic mode at all: sun_clock_warp and moon_clock_warp only A/B artifacts WITHIN the
default locked mode, so Patch_SunGlow had no live coverage before this.
Latitude 45 / day 37 is reused from moon_sun_clock.json for the same reasons: the moon is exactly
full at noon there (tick-derived cycle 0.5000, so this is not silently testing a gibbous moon),
and the two modes disagree about the day by the largest margin an ordinary colony sees —
LOCKED    vanilla's day, 18.06 h: sunrise 2.97, sunset 21.03
REALISTIC our physical day, 14.61 h: sunrise 4.69, sunset 19.31
The 1.73 h window between the two sunsets is where every discriminating probe below sits.
READ THE MOON AND SUN TOGETHER. The moon's elevation in realistic mode is numerically identical
to the moon_clock_warp=false BUG in locked mode (both put the moon on the raw percent), so a moon
reading alone proves nothing here. What separates them is the sun: in realistic mode the sun is
on the raw clock too, and in the bug it stays warped. That is why every moon_elevation probe
below is paired with sun_elevation at the same tick.
Every expected value was computed offline from the same pure cores the mod runs (MoonMath +
SunClockMath + Formulas), including the moon's phase drift across the day, and the model was
first calibrated by reproducing all eleven of moon_sun_clock.json's published values exactly.

steps._comment: Guard against a vacuous run: if this is not a full moon, nothing below means anything.
CONTROL. Midnight is a fixed point of the warp, so a mode change must move neither body by anything at all. This is what makes the mode a TIME WARP rather than a blanket offset applied to the sun.

THE MONEY PROBE. Hour 20 sits between the two sunsets, so the modes genuinely disagree about whether it is night — and both bodies must cross together. Locked: sun 7.4 up (still day), moon 11.2 down. Realistic: sun 7.2 DOWN (night began at 19.31), moon 4.1 UP. A moon left on the other mode's clock would hold one of these two values while the sun took the other.

The visible consequence of the pair above, and the reason this is worth a screenshot: at the same tick, locked mode renders a lit afternoon and realistic mode renders a moonlit night with a moon shadow on the ground. The moon is 4.1 degrees up, past MoonShadowStrength's ~3 degree ramp, so the composed shadow colour is the saturated full-moon 0.752 documented on MoonShadowRenderProbe.

Realistic mode's own §14 contract, the same one moon_sun_clock.json asserts for locked mode: vanilla's sky and our sun must agree about day/night at every hour. In this mode that agreement comes from the opposite direction — Patch_SunGlow rewrites the glow FROM our sun — so a zero here is what says the rewrite is actually in force and the moon above was measured against a real dark sky.

Moonrise lands on realistic mode's sunset. Hour 19.5 is 12 minutes past it: the sky has just gone dark (sun 2.7 down) and the full moon is still 0.5 degrees BELOW the horizon, i.e. the shadow handoff is continuous rather than popping. This is the realistic-mode counterpart of the 0.83 degree single-clock residual the unit tests bound.

Non-regression: the mode must not have simply deleted the moon. Deep night in BOTH modes, so both put the moon well up and casting — realistic 26.4 degrees, locked 23.0. The render value is identical because MoonShadowStrength has saturated in both.

MUST BE LAST. realistic_day_length is a plain static with no per-scenario reset, so leaving it on would silently re-time every subsequent scenario's sun. The probe is the receipt that the mode really is back to the shipped default: at hour 3 vanilla is 2 minutes past sunrise and locked mode holds our sun at -0.58, just above the refraction horizon, where realistic mode would have it 15.4 degrees down.
